title: Trionic Array I
descriptionHtml:
You are given an integer array nums of length n.

An array is trionic if there exist indices 0 < p < q < n − 1 such that:

  • nums[0...p] is strictly increasing,
  • nums[p...q] is strictly decreasing,
  • nums[q...n − 1] is strictly increasing.

Return true if nums is trionic, otherwise return false.

 

Example 1:

Input: nums = [1,3,5,4,2,6]

Output: true

Explanation:

Pick p = 2, q = 4:

  • nums[0...2] = [1, 3, 5] is strictly increasing (1 < 3 < 5).
  • nums[2...4] = [5, 4, 2] is strictly decreasing (5 > 4 > 2).
  • nums[4...5] = [2, 6] is strictly increasing (2 < 6).

Example 2:

Input: nums = [2,1,3]

Output: false

Explanation:

There is no way to pick p and q to form the required three segments.

 

Constraints:

  • 3 <= n <= 100
  • -1000 <= nums[i] <= 1000
explanationMarkdown:
> **Thinking**
>
> A trionic array is a nonempty strict rise, a nonempty strict fall, and another nonempty strict rise. Walking the three segments is simpler than enumerating two turning points.
>
> Pointer $p$ consumes the first ascent; stopping at the start fails. $q$ then consumes the descent; no movement or finishing at the end means a missing middle or last segment.
>
> The final ascent must end exactly at $n-1$. One pass checks existence and strictness of all three parts.

We first define a pointer $p$, initially $p = 0$, pointing to the first element of the array. We move $p$ to the right until we find the first element that doesn't satisfy strict increasing order, i.e., $\textit{nums}[p] \geq \textit{nums}[p + 1]$. If $p = 0$ at this point, it means the first part of the array doesn't have a strictly increasing section, so we return $\textit{false}$ directly.

Next, we define another pointer $q$, initially $q = p$, pointing to the first element of the second part of the array. We move $q$ to the right until we find the first element that doesn't satisfy strict decreasing order, i.e., $\textit{nums}[q] \leq \textit{nums}[q + 1]$. If $q = p$ or $q = n - 1$ at this point, it means the second part of the array doesn't have a strictly decreasing section or there's no third part, so we return $\textit{false}$ directly.

If all the above conditions are satisfied, it means the array is trionic, and we return $\textit{true}$.

The time complexity is $O(n)$, and the space complexity is $O(1)$, where $n$ is the length of the array.
